extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, and students of poetics / literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing and judging tragic (dramatic) poetry: plot/plot-unity, incidents, peripeteia/anagnorisis, passions, and formal parts of tragedy. Focuses on what makes a tragedy effective (pity/fear, causal surprise, structural parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Action must be entire and perfect and maintain unity; foreign or superadded episodes that do not form part of the Action corrupt its unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodick Fable ... which has something which is improper, foreign, and superadded, and which may be retrench'd without the Fables losing any thing. Such vicious Episodes are mostly found in simple Parts than others, so they furnish the Poet with less Matter, who is obliged to commit this irregularity. Example (anti-pattern): the Lie of Theseus and Dirce 'is not only no part of the Action, but it makes an Action by itself' and therefore is vicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adding episodes for actors' convenience (complaisance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets' complaisance to particular actors (making certain actors appear better) often forces them to multiply persons and corrupt the unity of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This complaisance 'obliges him oftentimes to forsake his Matter ... Multiplying the Number of the Persons, is forc'd to Corrupt the Unity of the Action by loose Episodes.' Even if theatrical company rivalries are less today, similar complaisance still produces ill effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's definitional aim — terror and compassion (pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of an entire and perfect Action which is capable of exciting Terror and Compassion (pity and fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a dramatic action excites other passions (e.g., admiration) instead of terror and compassion, it fails the design of Tragedy (example: Corneille's Nicomedes ought to be excluded because it refines passions by admiration rather than pity/fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude 'admiration' as the primary tragic aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Admiration is not the proper design of Tragedy; admiration is more appropriate to the epic poem and does not substitute for terror and compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pieces that aim chiefly to stir admiration for virtue (thus creating hatred of vice) deviate from Aristotle's tragic purpose — 'this way of refining the Passions by Admiration, is in no Wise the design of Tragedy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents must be causally connected (produced one from another)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surprise required for tragedy must show incidents that are produced of one another — i.e., each incident should follow necessarily or probably from preceding incidents, not merely come one after another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasises the difference between incidents which 'arise one from another' and those which 'only come one after another'; an incident that merely follows another without causal relation cannot produce the proper tragic surprise or unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on pure chance/fortuitous accidents for surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprises that result from accidents without sensible causes (pure chance) are improper for tragedy because they lead spectators to attribute them to blind chance rather than to intelligible causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper accidents: 'a Man being Crush'd to Pieces by the fall of a House; or Killed by a Stone thrown at Random.' Such fortuitous accidents lack the 'marvellous' produced by causally-linked incidents and do not refine the passions as tragedy requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer marvellous surprises produced by linked incidents (or Providence-guided events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that seem to be directed by Providence or a particular design (though they may be chance) produce a greater marvellousness and are preferable for tragic surprise than purely fortuitous accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that things which 'seem to come to pass designedly, and by a particular direction, are always much more Surprizing and Wonderful.' Examples: Homeric surprises and Biblical narratives are praised for their marvellous, causally-linked incidents (e.g., the statue of Mytys crushing his murderer, which spectators join cause and effect and infer design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Implex (complex) fable — definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple fables: actions which, continued and united, end without Remembrance or Peripetie. Implex (complex) fables: those which have either a Peripetie (reversal) or a Remembrance (recognition), or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of simple fables: Ajax and Philoctete (Sophocles), Medea and Phaedra of Euripides. Complex examples: Oedipus and Electra. Choice between simple and complex must proceed from the constitution of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripetie (reversal) — definition and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripetie is a change of one fortune into another, contrary to what was expected; the finest reversals are those least expected and most surprising, provided they be necessary or probable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peripeties should arise from preceding incidents such that the reversal follows necessarily or probably (example: the Corinthian's news in Oedipus producing an inevitable reversal). Avoid contrivances that spoil a finer peripetie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remembrance / Anagnorisis — definition and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembrance is a change from ignorance to knowledge that produces either hatred or love in those whom the poet intends to make happy or miserable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best remembrance is that which is joined with the peripetie (as in Oedipus) and which immediately produces the reversal; remembrances must produce a real change of condition in principal persons, not be vain or confined to secondary characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred form: remembrance joined with peripetie
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective form of recognition is that which accompanies the reversal and immediately produces the tragic change of fortune for the principal characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle holds that 'the best Remembrance, is that which is found with the Peripetie' because it produces maximal pity/fear and resolves the plot powerfully (Oedipus is given as the model). Avoid remembrances remote from the peripetie that do not instantly change the hero's fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of remembrance (single, double, inanimate-object-based, deeds/omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembrances may be single (one person remembered by another), double (two persons who do not know each other come to remember one another), may involve inanimate tokens (horses, necklaces), or be memories of deeds done or omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If lesser kinds of remembrances are used, they should serve as means or preparation for the principal remembrance that produces peripetie; isolated trivial remembrances are vicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripetie and remembrance must proceed from the subject's constitution (necessity/probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both peripetie and remembrance ought to proceed from the very constitution of the subject so that what precedes them should produce them necessarily or probably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reversal/recognition is not drawn from the 'bottom of the Subject' it will not be necessary or probable and thus will be ineffective or vicious (the example of Heraclius' problematic remembrance is given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Passion (pathos) in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Passion (pathos) is an action which destroys some person or causes some violent pains — evident and certain deaths, torments, wounds, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passion is more essential to the subject than peripetie or remembrance; simple subjects may have passion without peripetie/recognition (examples: Ajax, Hecuba). 'Evident and certain' misfortunes are required to produce strong tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the 'marvellous' and spectators' causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'marvellous' in tragedy arises when spectators can see both causes and ends of incidents (incidents linked together), allowing them to infer design rather than blind chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts mere accidental surprise (which spectators attribute to chance) with marvels that produce a stronger psychological effect because spectators perceive cause-effect chains; Homer and Scripture are cited as exemplars of marvels so produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presenting purely fortuitous occurrences without accessible cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic incidents should not be rooted in blind chance (events without a sensible cause) because they do not allow spectators to make causal application and thus do not refine the passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of improper fortuitous accidents include a house falling and crushing a man or a stone killing by random throw; these lack the 'marvellous' borne of causal linkage and are therefore unsuitable for tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of Tragedy (quantity) — principal divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has four principal parts: the Prologue, the Episode(s), the Exode, and the Chorus. The Chorus is further divided into Parodos, Stasimon, and Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Prologue = the part seen before the entrance of the Chorus; Episode = that which is between the songs of the Chorus; Exode = all that is said after the Chorus has left off singing; Parodos = first discourse of the Chorus; Stasimon = song after Chorus has taken possession of the stage (without anapaests and trochees); Commos = lamentations the Chorus and actors make together. Quantity parts are fixed and separable, unlike parts of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus integration and types of chorus-song
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus participates in the action and its songs have structural functions: Parodos (entrance chorus), Stasimon (incorporated song after entrance), and Commos (shared lamentation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stasimon is sung 'after it has taken possession of the Stage, and is as it were incorporated in the Action' and is metrically distinct. Commos occurs when Chorus and actors lament together; not every tragedy contains all chorus parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripetie should be necessary or probable (not merely possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: While peripeties should be surprising (contrary to expectation), they must follow necessarily or probably from preceding incidents; the surprising element must not violate plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary: 'it is certain, that the Peripeties, Which are least expected, and most surprising, are the finest, provided they be either necessary or probable.' A reversal that is impossible or implausible is defective.
